hits.name: Andrew Ng
hits.text:
The OpenAI-Hugging Face hack was enabled by weak sandboxing. It is great that Nvidia is releasing open source tools for sandboxing AI agents. OpenWorker, our open-source agent harness supporting cybersecurity workflows, is proud to support this.

A sandbox gives an agent limited permissions. OpenWorker is building on Nvidia OpenShell and will support running each agent's commands inside a sandbox. Only the files relevant to the task go in. Secret API keys, your web browser login credentials, the ability to access arbitrary websites, are inaccessible to the agent by default. These restrictions are implemented in deterministic code rather than by prompting an LLM, which can make mistakes or be susceptible to prompt injections. Further, all actions are logged for monitoring and audit.

I'm grateful for @JensenHuang's leadership making AI agents more secure. OpenWorker (which @rohitcprasad and I are working on) will continue to improve security for agents.
hits.full_text:
The OpenAI-Hugging Face hack was enabled by weak sandboxing. It is great that Nvidia is releasing open source tools for sandboxing AI agents. OpenWorker, our open-source agent harness supporting cybersecurity workflows, is proud to support this.

A sandbox gives an agent limited permissions. OpenWorker is building on Nvidia OpenShell and will support running each agent's commands inside a sandbox. Only the files relevant to the task go in. Secret API keys, your web browser login credentials, the ability to access arbitrary websites, are inaccessible to the agent by default. These restrictions are implemented in deterministic code rather than by prompting an LLM, which can make mistakes or be susceptible to prompt injections. Further, all actions are logged for monitoring and audit.

I'm grateful for @JensenHuang's leadership making AI agents more secure. OpenWorker (which @rohitcprasad and I are working on) will continue to improve security for agents.
hits.hook: AndrewYNg — OpenAI–HF hack blamed on weak sandboxing; OpenWorker + Nvidia OpenShell
hits.draft_en:
The HF/OpenAI incident wasn’t a prompt failure. It was a permission failure.

@AndrewYNg: weak sandboxing enabled the hack; OpenWorker will run agent commands inside Nvidia OpenShell — only task files in, secrets/browser/arbitrary web out by default, enforced in deterministic code, fully logged.

Security checklist for agent harnesses:
→ sandbox ≠ “please don’t do bad things” in the system prompt
→ deny-by-default egress and secret mounts
→ audit every tool call; assume prompt injection will try
→ treat agent identity as a privileged user with a change window

If your agent can see the keys, it will eventually spend them.

IAM is the permission brochure. Agents write the real story.

THN: IAM can show what an AI agent is allowed to do — and miss what the agent actually does by chaining tools inside applications.

Control plane gap:
→ static role reviews ≠ runtime tool-chain telemetry
→ need session/action logs for agent tool use (Andrew Ng’s point, same day)
→ least privilege must include “least tools in the loop”
→ detect anomalous tool sequences, not just role grants

Authorize the graph of actions, not just the JSON role.

virals.text:
Peter Steinberger, the creator of OpenClaw, open-sourced his entire agent setup

The core idea is one folder that every agent on his machines reads from. 

A single AGENTS.MD holds his rules, and a script symlinks it into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and ~/.codex/AGENTS.md
This way Claude Code and Codex always follow the same instructions.

Every other repo gets one line at the top: 
READ ~/Projects/agent-scripts/AGENTS.MD BEFORE ANYTHING. 
Change a rule once and every project picks it up.

Skills work the same way. 69 of them live in one place, each with a short description the agent reads to decide what to load, and scripts/sync-skills links them into both agents.

Fork it, replace his rules with yours, and delete the skills you do not need. His AGENTS.MD is full of his own hosts and accounts.

6.6k stars, MIT - https://github.com/steipete/agent-scripts

virals.text:
OPENAI 🔥: Key insights from upcoming DevDay sessions. 

* This agenda is not public yet 

First, OpenAI will build Platform capabilities inside Codex, enabling users to develop plugins, agents, and apps right from a dedicated DevDay page, which is quite cool! 

Highlights from the agenda 👀

> Claw Labs "Join Peter Steinberger for a look at how agents can change the way open-source teams build."

> 🔥 Codex Game Studio "What makes a game easy for humans but hard for AI? Build one and put Codex to the test."

> 🔥 What Will You Build With Coding Agents That Don’t Quit? What engineering work deserves your time and tokens? Learn from a Codex run that spent more than 1,000 hours keeping builds and tests passing in a large shared codebase. See how this internal OpenAI agent had goals, subagents, and persistent plans that helped it investigate failures and coordinate fixes. 

> Codex Has Left The Laptop "As we move from delegating individual tasks to letting Codex tackle entire problems and goals on its own, it’s possible to harness the power of Codex wherever and however you work. "

> From Single Player to Multiplayer with Codex "Follow a 2am outage from the first Slack messages to a reviewed fix and an update for the team."

> What Comes After Loops?: Deep Dive Into Agentic Architecture "As models become more capable, agent architectures are changing. We'll trace the evolution from simple loops to collaborating agents, examine the design choices and model advancements behind that shift, and take a deep dive into what comes next."
